t: Check if There is a Path With Equal Number of 0's And 1's — Editorial
o: Every monotone (right/down) path from (0,0) to (m-1,n-1) has exactly m+n-1 cells, so the balance (#1s minus #0s) along any path is fully determined by how many 1s it contains. We must decide whether some path achieves balance 0 — which immediately requires m+n-1 to be even. In Example 1 the grid is 3x4, so paths have 6 cells; a path with three 0s and three 1s exists, hence true. In Example 2 all paths have 5 cells (odd length), so equality is impossible and the answer is false without any search. Constraints (m,n ≤ 100) allow an O(m·n·(m+n)) DP over cell × balance.
k: Any monotone path visits exactly m+n-1 cells; if that number is odd, return false immediately.
Track only the running balance (#1s − #0s), which ranges in [-(m+n-1), m+n-1]; a DP over (row, col, balance) suffices.
Balance parity is fixed by position: at cell (i,j) the balance equals (i+j+1) minus twice the number of 0s seen, so reachable balances at each cell share one parity.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force DFS over all paths
a.i: Enumerate every right/down path from (0,0) to (m-1,n-1) with recursion, accumulating the count of 1s (or the balance). Return true if any path ends with equal counts of 0s and 1s. This is exponential in the worst case but fine for tiny grids and makes the problem structure obvious.
s: If m+n-1 is odd, return false (path length can't split evenly).
DFS from (0,0) carrying the current count of 1s seen so far.
At each cell add its value to the count; when reaching (m-1,n-1), check whether count == (m+n-1)/2.
Recurse right and down when in bounds; OR the results together.
a.t: Exponential, roughly O(2^(m+n)) in the worst case — the number of monotone paths grows combinatorially.

a.i: Instead of enumerating whole paths, note that a partial path's future possibilities depend only on its endpoint and its current balance (#1s − #0s). So define dp[i][j][b] = true if some path from (0,0) to (i,j) has balance b. Transitions come from the top and left neighbors with balance shifted by ±1 depending on grid[i][j]. The answer is whether any b=0 state is reachable at (m-1,n-1). Since balance lies in [-(m+n-1), m+n-1], this is polynomial and easily fits constraints.
s: If m+n-1 is odd, return false.
Let B = m+n; use offset B so balance b maps to index b+B (range [1, 2B-1]).
Initialize dp[0][0][offset] = grid[0][0] == 1 ? +1 : -1 shift, i.e., mark balance ±1 accordingly.
For each cell in row-major order, for each reachable balance from top/left neighbors, set dp[i][j][b + delta] where delta = grid[i][j] ? 1 : -1.
a.t: O(m · n · (m+n)) — for each of the O(mn) cells we scan O(m+n) possible balance values.
a.sp: O(m · n · (m+n)) for the 3D DP table; reducible to O(n · (m+n)) by keeping only two rows.

w: In an interview, start with the observation that every path has exactly m+n-1 cells — this gives an instant false for odd lengths (Example 2) and shows why tracking just the balance is enough. Then present the DP over (cell, balance) as the optimal solution; brute-force DFS is only worth mentioning briefly as motivation. Common pitfalls: forgetting the odd-length early exit, off-by-one errors in the balance offset (use offset m+n rather than m+n-1 so index 0 stays unused), and double-counting the starting cell. Edge cases: 2x2 grids (shortest non-trivial case), all-zeros or all-ones grids (always false since length > 0 means balance ≠ 0 unless... actually always false because no 1s/0s mix evenly when one count is zero and length ≥ 3). Follow-ups: reconstruct an actual valid path (store parent pointers per balance), handle 4-directional movement (then BFS/DFS with visited states (cell, balance)), or ask for the minimum |balance| achievable.
